claim: Nematostella vectensis PGCs arise as paired endomesodermal cell clusters during early development between 4 and 8 days-post-fertilization (dpf).
source: The localized expression of the conserved germline genes vasa and piwi suggest that Nematostella PGCs arise during the metamorphosis of planula larvae into primary polyps between 4 and 8 days-post-fertilization (dpf; Figure 1A–D''; Extavour et al., 2005; Praher et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by cited references (Extavour et al., 2005; Praher et al., 2017) and references to Figure 1A-D''.

claim: Putative PGCs in Nematostella first appear as discrete clusters within the two primary mesenteries, in close proximity to the pharynx.
source: These cells first appear as discrete clusters within the two primary mesenteries, in close proximity to the pharynx (Figure 1B–D'').
evidence: The claim is supported by reference to Figure 1B-D''.

claim: Vas2 is co-expressed with piwi1 and piwi2 in the putative PGC clusters of Nematostella.
source: To follow the development of putative PGCs at higher spatio-temporal resolution, we generated a polyclonal antibody against Nematostella Vasa2 (Vas2) and used immunohistochemistry and fluorescent in situ hybridization to confirm that Vas2 was co-expressed with piwi1 and piwi2 in the putative PGC clusters (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A–L).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A–L.

claim: Tudor is enriched in putative PGC clusters of Nematostella.
source: Further supporting their germline identity, we also found that tudor was enriched in putative PGC clusters (Figure 1—figure supplement 1M–P; Boswell and Mahowald, 1985; Arkov et al., 2006; Chuma et al., 2006).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1M–P and cited references (Boswell and Mahowald, 1985; Arkov et al., 2006; Chuma et al., 2006).

claim: The median number of Vas2+ cells per primary polyp in Nematostella is 10 cells.
source: We next quantified the number of putative PGCs in primary polyps and found that Vas2+ cell numbers varied between individuals, with a median number of 10 cells per primary polyp (Figure 1E).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantification data shown in Figure 1E.

claim: There is no significant difference in Vas2+ cell numbers between the two primary mesenteries of Nematostella.
source: We did not observe a significant difference in Vas2+ cell numbers between two primary mesenteries (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: There is no significant difference in the number of putative PGCs in primary polyps assayed on different days within the same spawning batch.
source: Within the same spawning batch, there was no significant difference in the number of putative PGCs in primary polyps assayed on different days.
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis of data from Figure 1E.

claim: There is neither loss nor expansion of PGCs in primary polyps prior to feeding and development of the juvenile stage.
source: This suggests that there was neither loss nor expansion of PGCs in primary polyps prior to feeding and development of the juvenile stage.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that PGC numbers do not change significantly over time in primary polyps.

claim: Adult Nematostella harbor mature gonads in all eight internal mesentery structures.
source: Adult Nematostella harbor mature gonads in all eight internal mesentery structures while confocal images found that Vas2+ epithelial cell clusters were localized only at endomesodermal septa associated with segments s2 and s8 (Figure 2A–B'; Video 1; Figure 2—figure supplement 1; Williams, 1975; Frank and Bleakney, 1976; He et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by confocal imaging data (Figure 2A–B', Video 1, Figure 2—figure supplement 1) and cited references (Williams, 1975; Frank and Bleakney, 1976; He et al., 2018).

claim: Vas2+ epithelial cell clusters in Nematostella are localized only at endomesodermal septa associated with segments s2 and s8.
source: Adult Nematostella harbor mature gonads in all eight internal mesentery structures while confocal images found that Vas2+ epithelial cell clusters were localized only at endomesodermal septa associated with segments s2 and s8 (Figure 2A–B'; Video 1; Figure 2—figure supplement 1; Williams, 1975; Frank and Bleakney, 1976; He et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by confocal imaging data (Figure 2A–B', Video 1, Figure 2—figure supplement 1) and cited references (Williams, 1975; Frank and Bleakney, 1976; He et al., 2018).

claim: In primary polyps older than 10 dpf, some PGC cluster cells appear to stretch basally through the underlying mesoglea.
source: In older primary polyps (>10 dpf), some PGC clusters cells appeared to stretch basally through the underlying mesoglea, an elastic extracellular matrix that separates epidermis and gastrodermis layers (Figure 2C–C'; Schmid, 1991; Shaposhnikova et al., 2005).
evidence: The claim is supported by imaging data (Figure 2C–C') and cited references (Schmid, 1991; Shaposhnikova et al., 2005).

claim: Upon feeding, Vas2-expressing putative PGCs in Nematostella appear to delaminate from the epidermis into the underlying mesoglea.
source: Interestingly, upon feeding, Vas2-expressing putative PGCs appeared to delaminate from the epidermis into the underlying mesoglea (Figure 2D–D').
evidence: The claim is supported by imaging data shown in Figure 2D–D'.

claim: Putatively delaminated Vas2 positive cells in Nematostella display a fibroblast-like morphology with pseudopodial protrusions.
source: Putatively delaminated Vas2 positive cells displayed a fibroblast-like morphology with pseudopodial protrusions, similar to other migratory cell types (Figure 2—figure supplement 2; Scarpa and Mayor, 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by imaging data (Figure 2—figure supplement 2) and a cited reference (Scarpa and Mayor, 2016).

claim: Vas2+ cells in Nematostella express twist.
source: Further consistent with migratory potential, Vas2+ cells also expressed twist (Figure 2—figure supplement 3), a conserved regulator of mesoderm development and a marker of metastatic cancer cells (Yang et al., 2004; Kallergi et al., 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by imaging data (Figure 2—figure supplement 3) and cited references (Yang et al., 2004; Kallergi et al., 2011).

claim: Twist is a conserved regulator of mesoderm development and a marker of metastatic cancer cells.
source: Further consistent with migratory potential, Vas2+ cells also expressed twist (Figure 2—figure supplement 3), a conserved regulator of mesoderm development and a marker of metastatic cancer cells (Yang et al., 2004; Kallergi et al., 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by cited references (Yang et al., 2004; Kallergi et al., 2011).

claim: There is a process of radial cell migration between mesenteries at the level of the aboral end of the pharynx in Nematostella.
source: While specification of additional PGC clusters was not observed on the six non-primary mesenteries, we did find evidence for a process of radial cell migration between mesenteries at the level of the aboral end of the pharynx, where the mesoglea between ectoderm and endomesoderm increases in volume after the primary polyp stage (Figure 2E–E').
evidence: The claim is supported by imaging data shown in Figure 2E–E'.

claim: The majority of 10 dpf primary polyps show PGCs within clusters.
source: The majority of 10 dpf primary polyps showed PGCs within clusters (Figure 3A–A'), while >10 dpf primary polyps showed some PGCs localized between the primary mesenteries and segment s1 (Figure 3B–B').
evidence: The claim is supported by imaging data shown in Figure 3A–A'.

claim: Primary polyps older than 10 dpf show some PGCs localized between the primary mesenteries and segment s1.
source: The majority of 10 dpf primary polyps showed PGCs within clusters (Figure 3A–A'), while >10 dpf primary polyps showed some PGCs localized between the primary mesenteries and segment s1 (Figure 3B–B').
evidence: The claim is supported by imaging data shown in Figure 3B–B'.

claim: The direction of initial PGC migration toward segment s1 suggests the existence of attractive/repulsive signals for migratory PGCs in Nematostella.
source: The direction of this initial migration toward segment s1 suggests the existence of attractive/repulsive signals for migratory PGCs.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observed directional migration pattern of PGCs.

claim: In juvenile Nematostella, putative PGCs migrate aborally toward the mesentery region where gonad rudiments will mature in adults.
source: Additionally, we found that in juveniles putative PGCs migrated aborally toward the mesentery region where gonad rudiments will mature in adults (Figure 3C–D').
evidence: The claim is supported by imaging data shown in Figure 3C–D'.

claim: Migratory PGCs in Nematostella are proliferative as shown by Phospho-Histone H3 labeling and EdU incorporation.
source: These migratory PGCs were proliferative as shown by Phospho-Histone H3 labeling and EdU incorporation (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: Putative PGCs in Nematostella initially form in primary polyps as two endomesodermal cell clusters at the level of the aboral pharynx.
source: Combining all observations, we hypothesize that in Nematostella, putative PGCs initially form in primary polyps as two endomesodermal cell clusters at the level of the aboral pharynx.
evidence: The claim is a hypothesis based on the combined observations presented in the manuscript.

claim: During juvenile stages, putative PGCs in Nematostella delaminate into the mesoglea layer between the ectoderm and endomesoderm via an apparent epithelial-mesenchymal transition (EMT) and then migrate to the gonad rudiments.
source: During juvenile stages, we further postulate that these cells delaminate into the mesoglea layer between the ectoderm and endomesoderm via an apparent epithelial-mesenchymal transition (EMT) and then migrate to the gonad rudiments.
evidence: The claim is a postulate based on the observations of cell morphology and localization changes.

claim: In maturing Nematostella polyps, the endomesodermal mesenteries are organized from proximal to distal into parietal muscles, retractor muscles, gonads and septal filaments.
source: In maturing polyps, the endomesodermal mesenteries are organized from proximal (external) to distal (internal) into parietal muscles, retractor muscles, gonads and septal filaments, with occasionally observed ciliated tracts between the gonads and septal filaments (Figure 4A–D; Williams, 1979; Jahnel et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by imaging data (Figure 4A–D) and cited references (Williams, 1979; Jahnel et al., 2014).

claim: In juvenile Nematostella polyps, Vas2+ cells are observed in the mesoglea between the septal filaments and the retractor muscles.
source: In juvenile polyps, Vas2+ cells were observed in the mesoglea between the septal filaments and the retractor muscles (Figure 4C), an endomesodermal region that will later form the adult gonad epidermis.
evidence: The claim is supported by imaging data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: After feeding for 8 weeks, most Nematostella polyps reach the 12-tentacle stage and the mesenteries progressively mature, becoming wider and thicker.
source: After feeding for 8 weeks, most polyps reached the 12-tentacle stage and the mesenteries progressively matured, becoming wider and thicker.
evidence: The claim is based on observations of developmental progression.

claim: At the 12-tentacle stage, Vas2+ putative PGCs are observed in the maturing gonad region, along with Vas2+ immature oocytes or sperm cysts in females and males, respectively.
source: At this stage we observed Vas2+ putative PGCs in the maturing gonad region, along with Vas2+ immature oocytes or sperm cysts in females and males, respectively (Figure 4E–F).
evidence: The claim is supported by imaging data shown in Figure 4E–F.

claim: In adult Nematostella mesenteries, putative PGCs are found in the vicinity of oocytes and sperm stem cells.
source: In adult mesenteries, similar putative PGCs were found in the vicinity of oocytes and sperm stem cells (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A–C') and in the aboral region of mesenteries (Figure 4—figure supplement 1D–E', and summarized in Figure 4—figure supplement 1F).
evidence: The claim is supported by imaging data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1A–C'.

claim: In the aboral regions of Nematostella mesenteries, Vas2+ PGC-like cells exhibit proliferative capacity as evidenced by EdU incorporation.
source: In the aboral regions, Vas2+ PGC-like cells exhibited proliferative capacity as evidenced by EdU incoporation (Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claim: The putative PGCs comprise a continuous Vas2-expressing lineage that proliferates and ultimately gives rise to mature germ cells in Nematostella.
source: Taken together, these observations suggest that the putative PGCs comprise a continuous Vas2-expressing lineage that proliferates and ultimately gives rise to mature germ cells.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the combined observations of Vas2+ cell localization and development.

claim: The germline gene-expressing cell clusters of primary polyps represent bona fide PGCs of Nematostella.
source: As proposed by previous work (Extavour et al., 2005), these data support the hypothesis that the germline gene-expressing cell clusters of primary polyps represent bona fide PGCs of Nematostella.
evidence: The claim is supported by the data presented and a cited reference (Extavour et al., 2005).

claim: Perinuclear Vas2 granules are distributed homogenously around oocyte germinal vesicles in Nematostella.
source: However, the perinuclear Vas2 granules were distributed homogenously around oocyte germinal vesicles (Figure 5A), in every cell of blastulae, and in most endomesodermal cells after gastrulation (Figure 5B; Praher et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by imaging data (Figure 5A) and a cited reference (Praher et al., 2017).

claim: Perinuclear Vas2 granules are present in every cell of blastulae in Nematostella.
source: However, the perinuclear Vas2 granules were distributed homogenously around oocyte germinal vesicles (Figure 5A), in every cell of blastulae, and in most endomesodermal cells after gastrulation (Figure 5B; Praher et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by imaging data (Figure 5B) and a cited reference (Praher et al., 2017).

claim: Perinuclear Vas2 granules are present in most endomesodermal cells after gastrulation in Nematostella.
source: However, the perinuclear Vas2 granules were distributed homogenously around oocyte germinal vesicles (Figure 5A), in every cell of blastulae, and in most endomesodermal cells after gastrulation (Figure 5B; Praher et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by imaging data (Figure 5B) and a cited reference (Praher et al., 2017).

claim: In endomesodermal cells, Vas2+ granules gradually diminish when the putative PGC cluster cells activate Vas2 expression.
source: In endomesodermal cells, Vas2+ granules gradually diminished when the putative PGC cluster cells activated Vas2 expression (Figure 5B–E''), suggesting that germ cell fate was gradually specified in endomesodermal precursor cells rather than being maternally predetermined in a set of germline precursor cells.
evidence: The claim is supported by imaging data shown in Figure 5B–E''.

claim: Germ cell fate in Nematostella is gradually specified in endomesodermal precursor cells rather than being maternally predetermined in a set of germline precursor cells.
source: In endomesodermal cells, Vas2+ granules gradually diminished when the putative PGC cluster cells activated Vas2 expression (Figure 5B–E''), suggesting that germ cell fate was gradually specified in endomesodermal precursor cells rather than being maternally predetermined in a set of germline precursor cells.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that Vas2+ granules diminish as PGC clusters form.

claim: Germline gene transcripts (vas1, vas2, nos2 and pl10) display a homogenous distribution in the endomesoderm of Nematostella embryos and larvae before PGC specification.
source: Furthermore, germline gene transcripts (i.e. vas1, vas2, nos2 and pl10) displayed a homogenous distribution in the endomesoderm of embryos and larva before PGC specification (Extavour et al., 2005).
evidence: The claim is supported by a cited reference (Extavour et al., 2005).

claim: Endomesodermal enrichment of germline genes before Nematostella PGC formation is consistent with the proposed germline multipotency program (GMP).
source: Endomesodermal enrichment of germline genes before Nematostella PGC formation could be consistent with the proposed germline multipotency program (GMP), where the expression of conserved germline factors underlies the multipotency of progenitor cells (Juliano et al., 2010).
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation of germline gene distribution and a cited reference (Juliano et al., 2010).

claim: Nematostella PGCs are specified from a pool of multipotent endomesodermal precursors.
source: In line with the GMP hypothesis, we hypothesized that Nematostella PGCs are specified from a pool of multipotent endomesodermal precursors as observed in other species that use zygotic mechanisms to induce PGCs.
evidence: The claim is a hypothesis based on the GMP model and observations in other species.

claim: Putative PGC clusters in Nematostella initially form in the two primary mesenteries.
source: In primary polyps, putative PGC clusters initially form in the two primary mesenteries, which are distinguished by the presence of aborally-extended regions of pharyngeal ectoderm known as septal filaments (Figure 6A–A', Video 1; Steinmetz et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by imaging data (Figure 6A–A', Video 1) and a cited reference (Steinmetz et al., 2017).

claim: Primary mesenteries in Nematostella are distinguished by the presence of aborally-extended regions of pharyngeal ectoderm known as septal filaments.
source: In primary polyps, putative PGC clusters initially form in the two primary mesenteries, which are distinguished by the presence of aborally-extended regions of pharyngeal ectoderm known as septal filaments (Figure 6A–A', Video 1; Steinmetz et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by imaging data (Figure 6A–A', Video 1) and a cited reference (Steinmetz et al., 2017).

claim: In Anthox6a mutants and Gbx shRNA-KD polyps, aberrant attachment of the septal filaments and the associated induction of PGC clusters in non-primary septa are observed.
source: Interestingly, segmentation of the presumptive primary mesenteries is disrupted in both Anthox6a mutants and Gbx shRNA-KD polyps (He et al., 2018). In both of these conditions, we observed aberrant attachment of the septal filaments and the associated induction of PGC clusters in non-primary septa (Figure 6B–D').
evidence: The claim is supported by imaging data (Figure 6B–D') and a cited reference (He et al., 2018).

claim: The precise location of the putative PGC clusters in Nematostella can be subject to regulation.
source: This suggests that the precise location of the putative PGC clusters can be subject to regulation, and hints at the existence of zygotic PGC-inducing signals from the pharyngeal ectoderm.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that PGC clusters can form in non-primary septa under certain conditions.

claim: There exist zygotic PGC-inducing signals from the pharyngeal ectoderm in Nematostella.
source: This suggests that the precise location of the putative PGC clusters can be subject to regulation, and hints at the existence of zygotic PGC-inducing signals from the pharyngeal ectoderm.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that PGC clusters form in association with pharyngeal ectoderm-derived structures.

claim: In late planula larvae, hedgehog1 (hh1) and patched (ptc) are expressed in reciprocal domains of ectoderm and endomesoderm associated with the pharynx.
source: Using double fluorescent in situ hybridization to detect the expression of Nematostella hedgehog1 (hh1) and its receptor patched (ptc) in late planula larvae, we found that both ligand and receptor were expressed in reciprocal domains of ectoderm and endomesoderm associated with the pharynx (Figure 7A).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7A.

claim: PGC clusters in Nematostella appear within the endomesodermal ptc expression domain, adjacent to where hh1 is expressed in the pharyngeal ectoderm.
source: Later, the PGC clusters appeared within the endomesodermal ptc expression domain, adjacent to where hh1 is expressed in the pharyngeal ectoderm (Figure 7B–D').
evidence: The claim is supported by imaging data shown in Figure 7B–D'.

claim: Hh signaling may direct neighboring endomesodermal cells to assume PGC identity in Nematostella.
source: Because PGCs formed in association with the juxtaposed hh1 and ptc expression domains, we hypothesized that Hh signaling may direct neighboring endomesodermal cells to assume PGC identity (Figure 7E).
evidence: The claim is a hypothesis based on the spatial relationship between hh1/ptc expression and PGC formation.

claim: PGC formation in Nematostella is impaired by hh1 or gli shRNA knockdown.
source: Using the expression of Vas2 protein and piwi1 transcripts as readouts for PGC identity, we found that PGC specification was significantly inhibited in both knockdown (Figure 7F–J) and presumptive F0 mutant primary polyps (Figure 7K–M; see Figure 7—figure supplement 1 and Materials and methods for gli gRNA target sites).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7F–J.

claim: PGC formation in Nematostella is impaired in presumptive F0 gli mutant primary polyps.
source: Using the expression of Vas2 protein and piwi1 transcripts as readouts for PGC identity, we found that PGC specification was significantly inhibited in both knockdown (Figure 7F–J) and presumptive F0 mutant primary polyps (Figure 7K–M; see Figure 7—figure supplement 1 and Materials and methods for gli gRNA target sites).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7K–M.

claim: The Hh signaling pathway is required for normal Nematostella PGC specification.
source: These data suggest that the Hh signaling pathway is required for normal Nematostella PGC specification.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the combined results of knockdown and mutagenesis experiments.

claim: PGC numbers in Nematostella are significantly reduced when early gastrulae are treated with the Smo antagonist GDC-0449.
source: When early gastrulae were treated with either inhibitor, we did not observe significant developmental defects at our working concentration (Figure 8A–D). However, PGC numbers were significantly reduced (Figure 8E–H).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 8E–H.

claim: PGC numbers in Nematostella are significantly reduced when early gastrulae are treated with Cyclopamine.
source: When early gastrulae were treated with either inhibitor, we did not observe significant developmental defects at our working concentration (Figure 8A–D). However, PGC numbers were significantly reduced (Figure 8E–H).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 8E–H.

claim: PGC formation in Nematostella is significantly inhibited by GDC-0449 treatment during 4 to 8 dpf metamorphosis.
source: Consistently, PGC formation was significantly inhibited by GDC-0449 treatment during 4 to 8 dpf metamorphosis (Figure 8—figure supplement 1B, compare Ctrl and GDC).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 1B.

claim: PGC number in Nematostella shows no significant difference when the Hh pathway is inhibited after specification (after 8 dpf).
source: In contrast, PGC number showed no significant difference when the pathway was inhibited after specification (Figure 8—figure supplement 1B, compare Ctrl-Ctrl and Ctrl-GDC).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Hh signaling is required for PGC specification but not PGC maintenance in Nematostella.
source: Therefore, Hh signaling is not likely to be involved in PGC migration after the initial specification step.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the temporal inhibitor treatment experiments.

claim: The drug vehicle DMSO may have deleterious effects on PGCs after specification in Nematostella.
source: However, we observed significantly fewer PGCs in long-term control treatments (0.05% DMSO between 4–12 dpf, Ctrl-Ctrl) than in short-term controls (4–8 dpf, Ctrl). In wild-type primary polyps, there was no significant difference in mean PGC number between 8, 12 and 16 dpf primary polyps (Figure 1E). We therefore infer that the drug vehicle DMSO may have had deleterious effects on PGCs after specification.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the comparison of PGC numbers in different DMSO treatment durations.

claim: The PGC population in Nematostella can be dynamically replenished, potentially through cell proliferation.
source: Furthermore, when we compared no-inhibition, continuous-inhibition and released-from-inhibition conditions (Figure 8—figure supplement 1B, compare Ctrl-Ctrl, GDC-GDC and GDC-Ctrl), PGC numbers did not vary significantly. These observations suggest that even though the initial PGC specification is Hh dependent, the PGC population can be dynamically replenished, potentially through cell proliferation.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that PGC numbers can recover after inhibition is removed.

claim: Hh signaling is not likely to be involved in PGC migration after the initial specification step in Nematostella.
source: Additionally, we did not observe PGC migration defects in different combinations of GDC-0449 treatments. At 12 dpf we found that like control polyps, more than half of treated polyps still showed the expected PGC migration away from the clusters: 18 of 29 polyps in Ctrl-Ctrl; 18 of 30 polyps in Ctrl-GDC; 19 of 30 polyps in GDC-GDC; 16 of 30 polyps in GDC-Ctrl (p value of Chi-squared test comparing with Ctrl-Ctrl are 0.87, 0.92 and 0.5 respectively). Therefore, Hh signaling is not likely to be involved in PGC migration after the initial specification step.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that PGC migration is not affected by Hh pathway inhibition.

claim: hh1 homozygous mutant polyps exhibit a shorter body column and pronounced tentacle defects compared to wild-type siblings at 8 dpf.
source: In F2 progeny resulting from crosses between heterozygous F1 siblings, we observed developmental defects in primary polyps wherein body length was reduced by approximately 50% and the four primary tentacles failed to elongate and partially fused together (Figure 9A–C', Figure 9—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by imaging data shown in Figure 9A–C' and Figure 9—figure supplement 2.

claim: Homozygous hh1 mutants express lower levels of ptc compared to wild-type.
source: Consistent with a defect in Hh signal transduction, homozygous mutants expressed lower levels of ptc, a conserved Hh pathway target gene (Figure 9D–E').
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 9D–E'.

claim: Primary polyps homozygous for hh1 mutant alleles develop primary mesentery-like endomesodermal septa.
source: Primary polyps homozygous for either hh1 mutant allele developed primary mesentery-like endomesodermal septa; however, we did not observe Vas2, piwi1 or tudor expressing PGC-like cluster cells (Figure 9F–I').
evidence: The claim is supported by imaging data shown in Figure 9F–I'.

claim: Vas2, piwi1 or tudor expressing PGC-like cluster cells are not observed in primary polyps homozygous for hh1 mutant alleles.
source: Primary polyps homozygous for either hh1 mutant allele developed primary mesentery-like endomesodermal septa; however, we did not observe Vas2, piwi1 or tudor expressing PGC-like cluster cells (Figure 9F–I').
evidence: The claim is supported by imaging data shown in Figure 9F–I'.

claim: In hh1 mutants, part of the pharynx and the primary septal filaments are in direct contact with the ectoderm.
source: In wild-type animals, the pharynx and primary septal filaments are separated from body wall ectoderm by intervening endomesodermal tissue (Figure 10A–A'). By contrast, in hh1 mutants part of the pharynx and the primary septal filaments were in direct contact with the ectoderm (Figure 10B–B').
evidence: The claim is supported by imaging data shown in Figure 10B–B'.

claim: In hh1 mutants, the eight segments of the larval body plan are abnormally segregated into groups of three and five segments by the pharynx.
source: As a result, the eight segments of the larval body plan were abnormally segregated into groups of three and five segments by the pharynx (Figure 10B).
evidence: The claim is supported by imaging data shown in Figure 10B.

claim: The endomesodermal patterning defects observed in hh1 mutants are not observed in hh1 and gli shRNA knockdowns.
source: These defects were not observed in hh1 and gli shRNA knockdowns, suggesting that PGC formation may require a higher level of Hh signaling activity than endomesoderm patterning.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the comparison of phenotypes between mutants and knockdowns.

claim: PGC formation may require a higher level of Hh signaling activity than endomesoderm patterning in Nematostella.
source: These defects were not observed in hh1 and gli shRNA knockdowns, suggesting that PGC formation may require a higher level of Hh signaling activity than endomesoderm patterning.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that PGC defects occur in knockdowns while patterning defects do not.

claim: Zygotic signaling activity is required for specification of the putative PGC clusters in Nematostella.
source: Nevertheless, without more sophisticated genetic tools, we cannot rule out the possibility that PGC formation was indirectly perturbed by Hh-dependent endomesodermal patterning defects. In either case, we conclude that zygotic signaling activity is required for specification of the putative PGC clusters.
evidence: The claim is a conclusion based on the combined results of mutant and knockdown experiments.

claim: Homozygous ptc mutants lack the four primary tentacles and do not develop the normal polyp body plan at the primary polyp stage (12 dpf).
source: Crosses between heterozygous siblings resulted in the expected 25% of homozygous progeny based on genotypic analysis, and these developed into abnormal mushroom-shaped polyps which lacked the four primary tentacles (Figure 10C–D, Figure 10—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by imaging data shown in Figure 10C–D and Figure 10—figure supplement 2.

claim: ptc homozygous mutants develop a pharynx, eight endomesoderm mesenteries, and two PGC clusters.
source: Detailed morphological examination and Vas2 immunofluorescence revealed that the ptc homozygous mutants developed a pharynx, eight endomesoderm mesenteries, and two PGC clusters (Figure 10D–E').
evidence: The claim is supported by imaging data shown in Figure 10D–E'.

claim: The presence of Hh ligand or absence of ptc activates the Hh pathway in Nematostella.
source: Combined with the requirement for hh1, gli and Smo activity during PGC specification, we propose that the presence of Hh ligand or absence of ptc activates the pathway and that zygotic Hh signaling provides permissive conditions for PGC formation within the pharyngeal domain of the Nematostella endomesoderm.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the combined results of hh1, gli, Smo, and ptc experiments.

claim: Zygotic Hh signaling provides permissive conditions for PGC formation within the pharyngeal domain of the Nematostella endomesoderm.
source: Combined with the requirement for hh1, gli and Smo activity during PGC specification, we propose that the presence of Hh ligand or absence of ptc activates the pathway and that zygotic Hh signaling provides permissive conditions for PGC formation within the pharyngeal domain of the Nematostella endomesoderm.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the combined results of hh1, gli, Smo, and ptc experiments.

claim: Hh signaling is required for both PGC specification and general endomesodermal patterning in Nematostella.
source: We then show that the PGC clusters arise at the interface between hedgehog1 and patched domains in the developing mesenteries and use gene knockdown, knockout and inhibitor experiments to demonstrate that Hh signaling is required for both PGC specification and general endomesodermal patterning.
evidence: The claim is supported by the combined results of knockdown, knockout, and inhibitor experiments.

claim: The Nematostella germline is specified by inductive signals rather than maternal factors.
source: These results provide evidence that the Nematostella germline is specified by inductive signals rather than maternal factors, and support the existence of zygotically-induced PGCs in the eumetazoan common ancestor.
evidence: The claim is a conclusion based on the combined results presented in the manuscript.

claim: Zygotically-induced PGCs existed in the eumetazoan common ancestor.
source: These results provide evidence that the Nematostella germline is specified by inductive signals rather than maternal factors, and support the existence of zygotically-induced PGCs in the eumetazoan common ancestor.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation of inductive PGC specification in Nematostella and its phylogenetic position.

claim: Nematostella employs an inductive mechanism to specify PGC fate.
source: We also demonstrate that putative PGCs form between the expression domains of hh1 and ptc and present evidence that Hh signaling is required for PGC specification but not PGC maintenance. Because Hh signaling transducers are only expressed zygotically (Matus et al., 2008; Lotan et al., 2014), these data indicate that Nematostella employs an inductive mechanism to specify PGC fate, which is consistent with the proposed ancestral mechanism for metazoan PGC specification (Extavour and Akam, 2003).
